CUSUM adds up how far each reading strays from its target. Small shifts that no single reading would catch still pile up, so it spots a slow, steady change early, like the start of an outbreak. Click through the vaccine line in @fig-cusum-line: each vial is measured, and the CUSUM climbs until it signals.

::: {#fig-cusum-line}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-cusum-line"></div>
```

A vaccine filling line with a target of 3.0 mL. Each vial adds its fill minus 3.05 mL (the target plus a slack $K = 0.05$ mL) to the CUSUM, which never drops below 0, and the line stops once the CUSUM reaches $H = 0.5$. Somewhere after vial 3 the filler starts to overfill by 0.18 mL, too little to stand out in any single vial. The fills are simulated.
:::

E.S. Page invented CUSUM in 1954 for factory quality control [@page1954]. Tillett and Spencer brought it into disease surveillance in 1982, with weekly influenza "cusum graphs" for England and Wales [@tillett1982]. Page tracked one parameter of a distribution, usually the mean, and set a rule for when a change was big enough to act on.

## Computing an epidemic threshold with CUSUM

For weekly case counts, the standard tool is the CUSUM in R's `surveillance` package ([`algo.cusum`](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/surveillance/versions/1.25.0/topics/algo.cusum)) [@rossi1999], building on counted-data CUSUMs [@lucas1985]. It runs in three steps, using the package defaults.

::: {.algo-step}
**1. Expected level.** Take the in-control mean $m$, the count you expect in a normal week. By default the package uses the mean of the weeks before monitoring starts.
:::

::: {.algo-step}
**2. Standardise.** Turn each count into a standardised deviation,

$$ z_t = \frac{x_t - m}{\sqrt{m}}, $$

so a normal week sits near $z_t \approx 0$ whatever the size of $m$.
:::

::: {.algo-step}
**3. Accumulate.** Add up these deviations minus a reference value $k$, floored at zero, and signal once the sum reaches the boundary $h$:

$$ S_t = \max\!\left(0,\; S_{t-1} + (z_t - k)\right), \qquad \text{signal when } S_t \ge h. $$
:::

The defaults are $k = 1.04$ and $h = 2.26$, and $S_t$ is not reset after a signal, so a whole outbreak stays flagged.

The same rule reads as a threshold on the raw count. To see where that threshold comes from, look at the accumulate step at the exact moment a week trips the alarm. At that point $S_t = h$, and the running sum is positive, so the floor does nothing:

$$ h = S_{t-1} + (z_t - k). $$

Rearrange for the standardised deviation that just reaches the boundary:

$$ z_t = h + k - S_{t-1}. $$

Now put back $z_t = (x_t - m)/\sqrt{m}$ from step 2:

$$ \frac{x_t - m}{\sqrt{m}} = h + k - S_{t-1}. $$

Multiply through by $\sqrt{m}$ and add $m$ to isolate the count:

$$ x_t = m + \sqrt{m}\,(h + k - S_{t-1}). $$

Cases are whole numbers, so the smallest count that reaches the boundary is this value rounded up. A week signals exactly when

$$ x_t \ge U_t = \left\lceil m + \sqrt{m}\,(h + k - S_{t-1}) \right\rceil, $$

the package's `upperbound`. This $U_t$ is the **epidemic threshold in cases**. It starts high and falls as evidence builds, so a steady rise is caught even when no single week looks extreme. Hover across @fig-cusum-threshold to see each week's numbers.

::: {#fig-cusum-threshold}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-cusum-threshold"></div>
```

Simulated weekly cases. Weeks 1 to 13 set the expected count $m = 8$. From week 14 the CUSUM $S_t$ (bottom) builds up during the outbreak, and the case threshold $U_t$ (red dashed step, top) falls as it does. Weeks that signal are red. Hover over or tap a week to see its numbers.
